title: The whole Jaap
hookLine: all 199 stanzas take about fifteen to twenty minutes
last: ASANKH NAAV — MORE NAMES THAN STARS.

lines: THEN, ACROSS THE VALLEY, ALL OF IT.
cards: You've seen a cathedral, a gurdwara or a mountain in pieces. A photo of a doorway, a close-up of a carving, one window, one dome.

Then one day you stand across the valley, see the whole thing at once, and every piece makes sense where it sits. For four weeks you've looked at Jaap Sahib one window at a time. Today you step back across the valley.

teach.b: Here's the map. Recited at a steady pace, all one hundred ninety-nine stanzas take about fifteen to twenty minutes.
It opens with one big stanza, the chhappai, that clears the table: no mark, no caste, no lineage; king of kings; named by deeds.
Then the snake begins to glide, bhujang prayat: namastvam akaale, namastvam kripaale, salutation after salutation.

The meter shortens to the quick two-word steps of chachari: aroop hain, anoop hain, ajoo hain, abhoo hain. Further along, the language turns to Persian and Arabic: the lamp of beauty, the giver of daily bread.
Longer rolling lines, roaal, bring one form, many sights.

teach.h: TINY LINES, ONE LETTER, THE GLIDE AGAIN.
teach.b: The tiny harbolmana lines give the home of compassion and the breaker of the cruel. The one-letter meter flies: ajai, alai, abhai, abai. Between them, other meters you haven't met yet, each with its own walk.
And the end returns to the glide, gathering everything into sadaa sachidaanand, and the last words, ever by your side. Seen whole, the shape is clear.

teach.h: WHAT HE ISN'T, WHAT HE IS, HE'S HERE.
teach.b: It begins by saying what the One isn't, spends nearly two hundred stanzas on what the One does and is, in rhythm after rhythm and more than one language, and ends by saying the One is right here.

That's why many Sikhs say Jaap is best known not in pieces but said whole, every morning, until it lives in the body. The words you've learned, akaal, kripaal, aroop, abhai, are signposts along that road.

how: Many Sikhs recite the whole of Jaap Sahib every morning, from memory or a gutka, in about fifteen to twenty minutes, and many others listen to recordings while traveling or getting ready for the day.

the Name, the presence of the One

games.q: you've learned Jaap in pieces for four weeks. what do many Sikhs say is the best way to know it?
o: keep studying it one word at a time.
say it whole, every morning, until it lives in the body.
games.why: the pieces are signposts; the road is the whole hymn, said daily.

practice: If you can, start the whole Jaap now and let it play on past the bell; it takes about fifteen to twenty minutes. Don't translate; just notice the meters change, like a road turning from gravel to pavement to dirt.
When a word you know goes by, akaal, kripaal, abhai, smile at it.

wordCard.voice: Naam, name. One hundred ninety-nine stanzas: from no mark and no caste, through every meter and language, to ever by your side.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: naam, name, the Name; Jaap is a whole morning of names.

carryVoice: Your line: all the names. Each piece makes sense where it sits. Day three hundred sixty, done.
